assistant_rules.note: Help me plan and point out grammar fixes as suggestions I can accept or reject. Don't write or rewrite my sentences. I submit my own work.

assignments.title: Essay 1: A place that taught you something
assignments.prompt: Write about a place that taught you something, and make a claim about what it taught you. About 600 words.

assignments.title: Response paper 1: Sugar and the Atlantic economy
assignments.prompt: Using the course readings, explain why sugar became central to the Atlantic economy. About 500 words.

assignments.title: Essay 2: Should our city make buses free?
assignments.prompt: Take a position on a local policy question, argue for it and answer at least one objection. About 1,000 words in the final essay; bring a 400-word draft to peer review.

sentences.text: This essay is about my grandmother's kitchen in Kochi and what I learned there.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Every summer I spent three weeks with her, and most of each day happened in that kitchen.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: She cooked for twelve people without a recipe, she measured salt with the palm of her hand.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: When I asked how she knew it was enough, she said the food would tell me.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: I thought she was joking until I burned my first batch of appam.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Now I cook in a dorm kitchen with a timer and a phone.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: I still taste before I measure.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Her kitchen taught me that paying attention is a skill you can practise.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: In this paper I will discuss the reasons sugar became important in the Atlantic world.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: There were many reasons, including European demand, Caribbean land and the slave trade.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Demand in Europe grew quickly in the seventeenth century, sugar went from a luxury to an everyday food.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Planters in Barbados and Jamaica cleared land for cane, and they forced enslaved Africans to do the work.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Mintz argues that sugar changed what working people in England ate.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Taken together, these reasons explain why sugar mattered so much.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Last month the city council debated whether to make the 14 and 22 bus lines free for riders.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Supporters packed the meeting, and so did a few business owners who were worried about the cost.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: This essay will look at both sides of the free-bus debate.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: I take the 22 to campus every morning, so I have seen who rides it and who does not.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Most mornings the bus is full before it reaches the hospital stop.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Fares are a bigger barrier than most people think, a monthly pass costs $64, which is more than many students spend on food in a week.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: A pass is cheaper per ride than single fares, but only if you can pay $64 at once.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: My roommate walks forty minutes to her job to save the fare, and some weeks she cannot afford the pass at all.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: When Riverton made its buses free two years ago, ridership went up.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: People who had stopped riding came back, especially older residents and part-time workers.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Free fares would also save drivers the time they spend making change.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: The main objection is cost.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Fares pay for about a fifth of the system, and the city would have to replace that money from somewhere.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: This is a fair point, and I understand why people worry about it.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Some council members said a small fee keeps riders respectful, I do not think that is true.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Most of the people I see on the 22 are tired, not rude.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Free buses would also help the environment.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: More riders means fewer cars downtown and less traffic near the hospital, where ambulances get stuck every afternoon.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: On my route I count at least ten cars for every bus at the Grant Street light.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: The council's own report says the downtown streets are already over capacity at rush hour.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Cleaner air matters to everyone who lives near Grant Street.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: In conclusion, there are good arguments on both sides.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Free buses cost money, but so do cars, parking and missed shifts.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: Students, nurses and part-time workers would feel the difference first.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: I think the city should try free buses on the 14 and 22 for one year and count who rides.
sentences.author: student

sentences.text: If ridership grows the way it did in Riverton, the council will have its answer.
sentences.author: student

comments.quote: This essay is about my grandmother's kitchen in Kochi and what I learned there.
comments.text: This tells me the topic, not what you learned. Your last sentence holds the real claim; could the essay start from it?

replies.author: student
replies.text: Thanks, I'll start from the claim next time.

comments.text: Comma splice: two complete sentences joined by a comma.

comments.quote: In this paper I will discuss the reasons sugar became important in the Atlantic world.
comments.text: You list causes but you do not argue. Which one mattered most, and why?

comments.quote: in the seventeenth century, sugar went

comments.text: Good use of the reading. Give the page number.

comments.quote: Free buses would also help the environment.
comments.text: This feels like a new topic. How does it connect to the fare argument?
I'm not sure what 'respectful' means here. Did someone actually say this?

comments.quote: This essay will look at both sides of the free-bus debate.
comments.text: This announces a topic again, as in Essay 1. What do you want the council to do, and why? Your conclusion already has the answer.
By how much, and how do you know? Name the source.
You name the objection but never answer it. Where would the money come from?

comments.quote: there are good arguments on both sides
comments.text: Here is your real position: a one-year trial. Lead with it in the first paragraph.

comments.quote: most people think, a monthly pass
comments.text: Comma splice: these are two sentences. Try a period or a semicolon.
Another comma splice, the same pattern as in paragraph 2.

comments.quote: Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more.
comments.text: The last sentence raises a new problem. Develop it or cut it.

messages.author: instructor
messages.text: Welcome to English 110. You may use AI tools to plan and organize your work and to talk through your drafts, but not to suggest or write wording. Ask me if you are unsure.

messages.author: student
messages.text: Can I use an AI tool to turn your comments into a checklist?

messages.author: instructor
messages.text: Yes, that is planning. The sentences in the essay have to be yours.

messages.text: AI tools may help with planning and with grammar or wording suggestions that you review yourself. The ideas and the argument must be yours.
